title: PostgreSQL DBA Part 23: Log Slow Queries with auto_explain
description: Log slow queries in PostgreSQL 18 on Ubuntu: log_min_duration_statement, log_line_prefix, lock waits, temp files and auto_explain, with real log output.

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: 19.8 Error Reporting and Logging
PostgreSQL 18 docs: 19.11 Client Connection Defaults (session_preload_libraries, shared_preload_libraries)

reviewNotes: Series part 23. Publish Part 22 first (Parts 19-22 are also not live yet; Part 22 is named without a link and is not in related). TEST ENVIRONMENT: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS with PostgreSQL 18.7 (18.7-1.pgdg24.04+5) from the official PGDG apt repository; all outputs in the article are real from this server. Documentation followed: PostgreSQL 18 docs (/docs/18/; postgresql.org/docs/current now shows version 19, so sources point to /docs/18/). Sandbox workaround: postgresql-18 depends on liburing2 from the Ubuntu archive, which the sandbox network blocks, so a local stub liburing2 package was installed to satisfy the dependency; the server ran with the default io_method = worker, so io_uring was never used and nothing in this article depends on it. Other sandbox differences: the sandbox also had an old, stopped 16 main cluster, so the pg_lsclusters output in Step 2 shows only the 18 line (as on a clean install); the 18 cluster was created on port 5433 and moved to 5432 before testing. No systemd in the sandbox, so reloads were done with SELECT pg_reload_conf() and sudo pg_ctlcluster 18 main reload; the article shows sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main as the equivalent. Step 1 was run non-interactively; the 'You are now connected' line was checked by running the same statement types in a throwaway database. Facts to check: log_connections became a list of options in PostgreSQL 18 (verified on the 18 logging page and in the test); log_checkpoints default on since PostgreSQL 15 is from the 15 release notes as remembered, not re-fetched. Plan outputs in Steps 9 and 11 use tabs in the real log; tabs were converted to two spaces for mobile, and the captions say so. The demo password Shop#2026 appears in the log_statement example on purpose, to show the leak.

data.text: This is Part 23 of the PostgreSQL DBA series, and the first part of the monitoring and performance section. In Part 22 we tested backups with restore drills. Now we turn to the question every DBA hears sooner or later: "the application is slow, which query is it?"

The quickest way to log slow queries in PostgreSQL is one setting: log_min_duration_statement. Set it to, say, 250ms, reload the configuration, and every statement that runs for 250 milliseconds or longer is written to the server log with its duration and its SQL text. Add the auto_explain module and the log also shows the execution plan of the slow statement, so you can see why it was slow.

By the end of this part you will know where PostgreSQL writes its log on Ubuntu, how to make every log line say who ran what from where, how to catch slow queries, lock waits and large temporary files, and how to turn on auto_explain safely. Every command and output was run on PostgreSQL 18 on Ubuntu.
What you will learn

items.content: Where the server log lives on Ubuntu, and why pg_current_logfile() returns nothing there
How to build a useful log_line_prefix that shows user, database, application and client address
How to log slow queries with log_min_duration_statement, for the whole server or for one role
Three more settings that catch real problems: log_lock_waits, log_temp_files and the PostgreSQL 18 options of log_connections
How to log execution plans of slow statements with auto_explain, and what it costs
How to find the slowest statements in the log with grep and sort

data.text: Prerequisites

items.content: Part 2 (PostgreSQL 18 installed from the PGDG repository on Ubuntu) and Part 5 (editing postgresql.conf, reload versus restart, pg_settings).
Part 10 (sessions and pg_stat_activity) helps for the lock wait example.
One Ubuntu server, called db1 in this part, running the cluster 18 main on port 5432. You need a user with sudo rights.
About 200 MB of free disk for a sample table with 2 million rows.

data.text: How it works

PostgreSQL writes messages about its own work to the server log: startup and shutdown, checkpoints, errors, and anything else you ask it to report. Think of it as the flight recorder of the database. By default it records very little about normal queries, so when something goes wrong at 3 a.m. the recorder was mostly switched off.
Logging settings answer three questions, and the documentation groups them the same way:

content: log_destination, logging_collector (and on Ubuntu, the pg_ctlcluster log file)
log_line_prefix, log_lock_waits, log_temp_files, log_connections, log_disconnections, log_statement

data.text: auto_explain is different. It is a module that ships with PostgreSQL (in the postgresql-18 package, no extra install). When a statement runs longer than its threshold, it writes the same plan you would get from EXPLAIN into the log. A plain slow query log tells you what was slow. auto_explain tells you why.

Most logging settings can be changed with a reload, which does not disconnect anyone. Only a few, such as logging_collector and shared_preload_libraries, need a restart. This part uses reload-only settings throughout.

data.code:
application (billing_app) --SQL--> PostgreSQL 18 on db1 (127.0.0.1:5432)
                                       |
                                       | slow statement, lock wait, temp file
                                       v
                        /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log
data.caption: Where the messages in this part end up

data.text: Sample setup
We need queries that are really slow, so the sample orders table gets 2 million rows. We also create a login role shop_app that plays the part of the application.
Step 1: Create the sample database, table and application role
On db1, as the postgres operating system user (through sudo), open psql and run:

data.code: sudo -u postgres psql

data.caption: Sample data: 2 million orders and an application role

data.code:
CREATE DATABASE
You are now connected to database "shop" as user "postgres".
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2000000
ANALYZE
CREATE ROLE
GRANT
data.caption: Output

data.text: The insert takes a few seconds. To verify, run SELECT count(*) FROM orders; and expect 2000000. To remove everything after the part, run DROP DATABASE shop; and DROP ROLE shop_app; as postgres.
Where PostgreSQL logs go on Ubuntu
Step 2: Find the log file and check the current settings
On db1, as a user with sudo. The Ubuntu packages start every cluster through pg_ctlcluster, which sends the server's messages to one file per cluster. pg_lsclusters shows its path in the last column:

data.code: pg_lsclusters

Ver Cluster Port Status Owner    Data directory              Log file
18  main    5432 online postgres /var/lib/postgresql/18/main /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log
data.caption: Output

data.text: Now look at the logging settings the cluster is using. Run this in psql as postgres:

data.code:
SELECT name, setting, unit, context
  FROM pg_settings
 WHERE name IN ('logging_collector', 'log_destination',
                'log_line_prefix', 'log_min_duration_statement',
                'log_lock_waits', 'log_temp_files',
                'log_autovacuum_min_duration', 'log_checkpoints',
                'log_statement')
 ORDER BY name;
data.caption: Current logging settings

data.code:
name             |     setting      | unit |  context
-----------------------------+------------------+------+------------
 log_autovacuum_min_duration | 600000           | ms   | sighup
 log_checkpoints             | on               |      | sighup
 log_destination             | stderr           |      | sighup
 log_line_prefix             | %m [%p] %q%u@%d  |      | sighup
 log_lock_waits              | off              |      | superuser
 log_min_duration_statement  | -1               | ms   | superuser
 log_statement               | none             |      | superuser
 log_temp_files              | -1               | kB   | superuser
 logging_collector           | off              |      | postmaster
(9 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: What this shows:

items.content: logging_collector is off and log_destination is stderr. PostgreSQL writes to standard error, and pg_ctlcluster sends that to /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log. That is why SELECT pg_current_logfile(); returns an empty (NULL) result on Ubuntu: the function only reports files written by the logging collector.
log_min_duration_statement is -1, the documented default, which means statement durations are not logged at all.
log_checkpoints is already on (the default since PostgreSQL 15) and autovacuum actions that take 10 minutes or more are logged (600000 ms is the default 10min).

The context column tells you how a setting can change. sighup means a reload is enough, superuser means a reload works and a superuser can also change it per session, and postmaster means restart only.

data.text: To follow the log live while you work through this part, open a second terminal on db1 and run sudo tail -f /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log. Ubuntu rotates this file weekly and keeps 10 compressed copies, set in /etc/logrotate.d/postgresql-common.

data.title: Should you turn on logging_collector?
data.text: On Ubuntu you usually do not need to. The packaged setup with logrotate works well and keeps logs under /var/log/postgresql, where your other tools look. If you do set logging_collector = on, it needs a restart, and the files then go to log_directory (default log, inside the data directory) instead of /var/log/postgresql.
Make every log line useful with log_line_prefix

A log line without context is hard to act on. ERROR: column does not exist is only useful if you know which application, user and database sent it. log_line_prefix is a printf-style string written at the start of every line; each % escape is replaced with a piece of session information.
Step 3: Add the application name and client address to the prefix
On db1, as a user with sudo, open /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf in an editor (sudo nano /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf) and change the log_line_prefix line:

data.code:
# before (Ubuntu package default)
log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d '

# after
log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d app=%a client=%h '
data.caption: /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf

data.text: What each escape means, from the documentation's table:

content: Process ID of the server process
Nothing; tells background processes (which have no user or database) to stop printing the prefix here
Application name (set by the client, for example with application_name in the connection string)
Remote host name or IP address, or [local] for a Unix socket connection

data.text: The documented default of log_line_prefix is '%m [%p] '; the Ubuntu package adds %q%u@%d . Keep a space as the last character so the prefix is separated from the message. Other useful escapes are %c (session ID), %x (transaction ID) and %e (SQLSTATE error code). If you plan to use a log analyzer later, check which prefix format it expects before you change this.
The setting has context sighup, so reload. In psql as postgres:

data.code: SELECT pg_reload_conf();

pg_reload_conf
----------------
 t
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: t only means the reload signal was sent. The log confirms that the server read the new value:

data.code:
2026-11-23 12:48:41.162 UTC [2548] LOG:  received SIGHUP, reloading configuration files
2026-11-23 12:48:41.163 UTC [2548] LOG:  parameter "log_line_prefix" changed to "%m [%p] %q%u@%d app=%a client=%h "
data.caption: Output (from /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log)

data.text: Verify: open a new psql session and run SHOW log_line_prefix;. Then connect as the application and run a query with a mistake in it:

data.code:
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW log_line_prefix;"

psql "host=127.0.0.1 dbname=shop user=shop_app application_name=billing_app" \
     -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE undefined_col = 1;"

log_line_prefix
-----------------------------------
 %m [%p] %q%u@%d app=%a client=%h
(1 row)

2026-11-23 12:55:22.473 UTC [2969] shop_app@shop app=billing_app client=127.0.0.1 ERROR:  column "undefined_col" does not exist at character 35
2026-11-23 12:55:22.473 UTC [2969] shop_app@shop app=billing_app client=127.0.0.1 STATEMENT:  SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE undefined_col = 1;
data.caption: Output (SHOW result, then the new lines in the log; psql also prints the ERROR on screen)

data.text: Now the error line tells you the user, database, application and client address. The STATEMENT: line appears because log_min_error_statement defaults to ERROR: every statement that fails with an error is logged with its text.
Undo: put back log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d ' and reload.
Log slow queries with log_min_duration_statement

log_min_duration_statement logs the duration and the text of every completed statement that ran for at least the given time. A value without units is milliseconds, 0 logs every statement and -1 (the default) turns it off.

Choosing the threshold is a trade-off. Too low and the log fills with thousands of fast statements, costing disk space and some I/O. Too high and you miss the queries users complain about. A common starting point for an OLTP application is somewhere between 250 ms and 1 s; lower it later if the log stays quiet.
Step 4: Turn on slow query logging, lock wait logging and temp file logging
On db1, as a user with sudo, edit /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf. The three lines are commented out by default; remove the # and set the values:

data.code:
# before (defaults, commented out)
#log_min_duration_statement = -1       # -1 is disabled, 0 logs all statements
#log_lock_waits = off                  # log lock waits >= deadlock_timeout
#log_temp_files = -1                   # log temporary files equal or larger

# after
log_min_duration_statement = 250ms
log_lock_waits = on
log_temp_files = 10MB
data.caption: /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf

content: Logs every statement that runs 250 ms or longer, with its duration and text (default -1, off)
Logs a message when a session waits longer than deadlock_timeout (default 1s) for a lock (default off)
Logs each temporary file of 10 MB or more, with its size, when it is deleted. Sorts and hashes that do not fit in work_mem create these files (default -1, off)

data.text: All three can be changed with a reload. In psql as postgres:

data.code:
name            | setting | unit
----------------------------+---------+------
 log_lock_waits             | on      |
 log_min_duration_statement | 250     | ms
 log_temp_files             | 10240   | kB
(3 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: pg_settings shows the value in its base unit: 250 ms, and 10 MB as 10240 kB. The log also records each changed parameter, as in Step 3.
Step 5: Run a slow query and read the log entry
On db1, as any OS user, connect as the application and run one slow report and one fast lookup:

data.code: psql "host=127.0.0.1 dbname=shop user=shop_app application_name=billing_app"

data.text: The report took almost 3 seconds; the primary key lookup took under 1 ms. Now look at the log (sudo tail -3 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log):

data.caption: Output

data.text: Two settings fired for one statement:

items.content: The duration: line comes from log_min_duration_statement. It gives the exact time and the full SQL text. The fast lookup is not in the log, which is what you want.

The temporary file: line comes from log_temp_files. The sort for count(DISTINCT ...) needed about 42 MB on disk (44097536 bytes), because it did not fit in work_mem (default 4 MB). Temp files are a strong hint that a query needs a better plan, an index or more memory, which Part 26 and Part 28 cover.

data.title: Statements sent with bind parameters
data.text: Most application drivers use the extended query protocol. For those, the documentation notes that the durations of the Parse, Bind and Execute steps are logged separately, and the log shows the bind parameter values. log_parameter_max_length (default -1, full values) controls how much of each value is written; set it to a small number, or 0, if parameters can contain personal data.
Step 6: See a lock wait in the log

Slow is not always a bad plan. Often a statement is simply waiting for another transaction to release a row lock. With log_lock_waits = on PostgreSQL tells you. On db1, open two terminals. In terminal A, update a row and keep the transaction open:

data.code:
-- terminal B (start while A is sleeping): psql "host=127.0.0.1 dbname=shop user=shop_app application_name=billing_app"
UPDATE orders SET amount = amount + 10 WHERE order_id = 42;

data.caption: Output (from /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log)

data.text: Read it from the top. After 1 second (the default deadlock_timeout) process 2711 reported that it was waiting, and the DETAIL line names the blocker, process 2709. The prefix shows that 2709 is the admin_console application. When the blocker committed, 2711 logged how long it waited in total. The 3-second UPDATE of a single row was not slow because of its plan; it was blocked. Part 29 covers locks in depth.
Step 7: Use a different threshold for one role or database

Only superusers (and roles granted SET on the parameter) can change log_min_duration_statement, so an application cannot switch it off for itself. A DBA can set it per role or per database with ALTER ROLE ... SET or ALTER DATABASE ... SET. On db1, in psql as postgres:

data.code:
ALTER ROLE shop_app SET log_min_duration_statement = '100ms';
\drds shop_app

ALTER ROLE
                    List of settings
   Role   | Database |             Settings
----------+----------+----------------------------------
 shop_app |          | log_min_duration_statement=100ms
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Verify: the value applies to new sessions of shop_app. Connect as shop_app and run SHOW log_min_duration_statement;; it returns 100ms. If shop_app itself tries SET log_min_duration_statement = 0; it gets ERROR: permission denied to set parameter "log_min_duration_statement".
Undo: ALTER ROLE shop_app RESET log_min_duration_statement;
Log connections and disconnections (new options in PostgreSQL 18)

In PostgreSQL 18, log_connections changed from on/off to a list of options: receipt, authentication, authorization, setup_durations and all. The old values still work: on means receipt, authentication and authorization. setup_durations is new and logs how long each connection took to set up, which helps when users say "connecting is slow".
Step 8: Log authorized connections, their setup time and disconnections
On db1, as a user with sudo, edit /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf:

data.code:
# before
#log_connections = ''                  # log aspects of connection setup
#log_disconnections = off

# after
log_connections = 'authorization,setup_durations'
log_disconnections = on
data.caption: /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf

data.text: Apply with sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main (or SELECT pg_reload_conf();). Both settings take effect for new sessions only; the documentation says they cannot be changed within a session. Then connect once as the application:

data.code:
sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main
psql "host=127.0.0.1 dbname=shop user=shop_app application_name=billing_app" -c "SELECT 1;" > /dev/null
sudo tail -3 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log

2026-11-23 12:52:23.273 UTC [2898] shop_app@shop app=[unknown] client=127.0.0.1 LOG:  connection authorized: user=shop_app database=shop application_name=billing_app SSL enabled (protocol=TLSv1.3, cipher=TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, bits=256)
2026-11-23 12:52:23.283 UTC [2898] shop_app@shop app=billing_app client=127.0.0.1 LOG:  connection ready: setup total=21.753 ms, fork=0.717 ms, authentication=5.048 ms
2026-11-23 12:52:23.284 UTC [2898] shop_app@shop app=billing_app client=127.0.0.1 LOG:  disconnection: session time: 0:00:00.022 user=shop_app database=shop host=127.0.0.1 port=37466
data.caption: Output

data.text: The connection ready line splits the setup time into fork and authentication. Notice app=[unknown] on the first line: at that moment the application name has not been applied yet, but the message itself includes it. On a busy server with many short connections these lines add up quickly, which is one reason to use a connection pooler (Part 30).
Undo: comment both lines out again and reload.
Log execution plans of slow queries with auto_explain

The slow query log told us the report took 2.9 seconds. To fix it you need the plan, and by the time you run EXPLAIN by hand the data, the parameters or the cached statistics may have changed. auto_explain captures the plan of the slow execution itself, at the moment it happened.
Step 9: Try auto_explain in your own session first

On db1, in psql as postgres, connected to shop. LOAD loads the module into this session only (superuser required). Nothing is logged until auto_explain.log_min_duration is set, because its default is -1.

data.code:
LOAD
SET
SET
 count
-------
    42
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.code:
2026-11-23 12:51:25.554 UTC [2723] postgres@shop app=psql client=[local] LOG:  duration: 43.550 ms  plan:
  Query Text: SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4711;
  Finalize Aggregate  (cost=27165.93..27165.94 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=40.074..43.532 rows=1.00 loops=1)
    ->  Gather  (cost=27165.71..27165.92 rows=2 width=8) (actual time=39.933..43.521 rows=3.00 loops=1)
          Workers Planned: 2
          Workers Launched: 2
          ->  Partial Aggregate  (cost=26165.71..26165.72 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=37.116..37.117 rows=1.00 loops=3)
                ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..26165.67 rows=18 width=0) (actual time=8.407..37.095 rows=14.00 loops=3)
                      Filter: (customer_id = 4711)
                      Rows Removed by Filter: 666653
data.caption: Output (from /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log; tabs shown as spaces)

data.text: The client sees only the result. The plan goes to the log. It shows a parallel sequential scan that read all 2 million rows to find 42, because there is no index on customer_id. The plan alone answers "why was it slow?". When you close this session, auto_explain is gone again.
Step 10: Turn on auto_explain for all new sessions
There are two ways to load the module for everyone, both documented:

content: If the library name is wrong
Reload; each NEW session loads it
Every new connection fails, including yours

data.text: session_preload_libraries avoids a restart, so we use it. Ubuntu's postgresql.conf ends with include_dir = 'conf.d', so instead of editing the main file you can put the settings in their own file and remove them later by deleting it. On db1, as a user with sudo, create /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/auto_explain.conf:

data.code: sudo -u postgres nano /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/auto_explain.conf

# auto_explain: log the plan of any statement that runs 1 second or longer
session_preload_libraries = 'auto_explain'
auto_explain.log_min_duration = '1s'
auto_explain.log_analyze = on
auto_explain.log_buffers = on
auto_explain.log_timing = off
data.caption: /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/auto_explain.conf (new file)

content: Minimum run time that causes the plan to be logged; 0 logs all plans (default -1, off)
Logs EXPLAIN ANALYZE output (actual rows and loops) instead of plain EXPLAIN (default off)
Adds buffer usage, like EXPLAIN (BUFFERS); works only with log_analyze (default off)
Per-node timing; works only with log_analyze. Off keeps actual row counts but skips the costly clock reads (default on)

data.title: log_analyze has a cost on every statement
data.text: The documentation warns that with auto_explain.log_analyze on, per-plan-node timing happens for all statements, whether or not they run long enough to be logged, and that this can have an extremely negative impact on performance. Turning off auto_explain.log_timing reduces that cost. On a busy production server, test the overhead first, start with log_analyze off, or use auto_explain.sample_rate to explain only a fraction of statements.
Apply with a reload, then check the values from a new psql session as postgres:

data.code: sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main

SELECT name, setting, unit
  FROM pg_settings
 WHERE name LIKE 'auto_explain%' OR name = 'session_preload_libraries'
 ORDER BY name;

name                  |   setting    | unit
---------------------------------------+--------------+------
 auto_explain.log_analyze              | on           |
 auto_explain.log_buffers              | on           |
 auto_explain.log_format               | text         |
 auto_explain.log_level                | log          |
 auto_explain.log_min_duration         | 1000         | ms
 auto_explain.log_nested_statements    | off          |
 auto_explain.log_parameter_max_length | -1           | B
 auto_explain.log_settings             | off          |
 auto_explain.log_timing               | off          |
 auto_explain.log_triggers             | off          |
 auto_explain.log_verbose              | off          |
 auto_explain.log_wal                  | off          |
 auto_explain.sample_rate              | 1            |
 session_preload_libraries             | auto_explain |
(14 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: All auto_explain.* rows appear because this new session loaded the module at connection start. Sessions that were already connected before the reload do not have it; they pick it up when they reconnect. log_nested_statements is off, so statements run inside functions are not explained; turn it on if your application logic lives in PL/pgSQL.
Step 11: Read the plan of a real slow query
On db1, run the slow report from Step 5 again as shop_app, then look at the log:

data.code:
psql "host=127.0.0.1 dbname=shop user=shop_app application_name=billing_app" \
     -c "SELECT status, count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers FROM orders GROUP BY status;" > /dev/null
sudo tail -14 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log

2026-11-23 12:51:45.825 UTC [2768] shop_app@shop app=billing_app client=127.0.0.1 LOG:  duration: 2836.017 ms  plan:
  Query Text: SELECT status, count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers FROM orders GROUP BY status;
  GroupAggregate  (cost=313426.69..328426.73 rows=4 width=14) (actual rows=4.00 loops=1)
    Group Key: status
    Buffers: shared hit=13492 read=2263, temp read=10765 written=10792
    ->  Sort  (cost=313426.69..318426.69 rows=2000000 width=10) (actual rows=2000000.00 loops=1)
          Sort Key: status, customer_id
          Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 43064kB
          Buffers: shared hit=13492 read=2263, temp read=10765 written=10792
          ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..35749.00 rows=2000000 width=10) (actual rows=2000000.00 loops=1)
                Buffers: shared hit=13486 read=2263
2026-11-23 12:51:45.828 UTC [2768] shop_app@shop app=billing_app client=127.0.0.1 LOG:  temporary file: path "base/pgsql_tmp/pgsql_tmp2768.0", size 44097536
2026-11-23 12:51:45.828 UTC [2768] shop_app@shop app=billing_app client=127.0.0.1 STATEMENT:  SELECT status, count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers FROM orders GROUP BY status;
2026-11-23 12:51:45.829 UTC [2768] shop_app@shop app=billing_app client=127.0.0.1 LOG:  duration: 2841.516 ms  statement: SELECT status, count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers FROM orders GROUP BY status;
data.caption: Output (from /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log; tabs shown as spaces)

data.text: Now the three log entries tell one story. The plan shows a full scan of 2 million rows feeding a sort, and Sort Method: external merge Disk: 43064kB says the sort spilled to disk, which matches the temporary file line. Because log_timing is off, nodes show actual rows without times, which is enough to see where the rows go. temp read/written in the Buffers lines counts 8 kB blocks of temporary files.
Undo: sudo rm /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/auto_explain.conf, then sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main. New sessions no longer load the module.
Find the slowest statements in the log
Step 12: List the top statements by duration
On db1, as a user with sudo. Every slow statement line contains duration: N ms statement:, so grep and sort are enough for a quick look:

data.code:
sudo grep -oE "duration: [0-9.]+ ms  statement: .*" /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log \
  | sort -t' ' -k2 -rn | head -5

content: Prints only the matching part of each line (-o), using an extended regular expression (-E)
Splits on spaces, sorts on the second field (the number of milliseconds), numeric (-n), largest first (-r)

data.caption: Output

data.text: This works for a quick check, but it lists single executions. A query that takes 50 ms and runs a million times a day never shows up here, and it may cost far more in total. That is exactly the gap pg_stat_statements fills in Part 25. The log and pg_stat_statements work best together.
Common mistakes and how to fix them
A typo in session_preload_libraries locks everyone out
If the library name is wrong, every new connection fails, including the postgres superuser on the local socket. We tested it with 'auto_explan':

data.code: psql: error: connection to server on socket "/var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432" failed: FATAL:  could not access file "auto_explan": No such file or directory
data.caption: Output

data.text: Fix: you cannot use SELECT pg_reload_conf(); because you cannot connect. Correct the file, then reload from the shell: sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main (or sudo pg_ctlcluster 18 main reload). Existing sessions keep working the whole time. To avoid this, test with LOAD 'auto_explain'; in a session first, as in Step 9.
A typo in shared_preload_libraries stops the server from starting

data.code:
Error: /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_ctl /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_ctl start -D /var/lib/postgresql/18/main -l /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log -s -o  -c config_file="/etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf"  exited with status 1:
2026-11-23 12:52:08.637 UTC [2833] FATAL:  could not access file "auto_explan": No such file or directory
2026-11-23 12:52:08.637 UTC [2833] LOG:  database system is shut down
pg_ctl: could not start server
Examine the log output.
data.caption: Output of sudo pg_ctlcluster 18 main restart

data.text: Fix: correct the name and run sudo pg_ctlcluster 18 main start. Before any restart in production, check with SELECT name, setting, error FROM pg_file_settings WHERE error IS NOT NULL; (which only catches syntax errors) and test the library with LOAD.
SHOW still returns the old value after pg_reload_conf()

pg_reload_conf() only sends a signal. In our test, SELECT pg_reload_conf(); followed by SHOW log_line_prefix; in the same psql call still returned the old prefix. Fix: check a moment later from a new session, or look for the parameter "..." changed to line in the log.
log_statement = 'all' or 'ddl' writes passwords into the log
log_statement logs statement text by type, and the documentation warns that logged statements might contain plaintext passwords. With log_statement = 'ddl':

data.code: 2026-11-23 12:52:16.487 UTC [2875] postgres@postgres app=psql client=[local] LOG:  statement: ALTER ROLE shop_app PASSWORD 'Shop#2026';
data.caption: Output

data.text: Fix: set passwords with psql's \password shop_app, which sends an already encrypted password. Keep the log file private (Ubuntu creates it with mode 0640, owner postgres, group adm). For real auditing use pgaudit, covered in Part 42.
log_min_duration_statement = 0 on a busy server

Setting it to 0 logs every statement. On a server running thousands of statements a second this can fill the disk and slow the server down. Fix: use it only for a short, planned period, or use log_min_duration_sample with log_statement_sample_rate to log a random fraction of statements above a lower threshold.
Practice exercise

items.content: Make PostgreSQL log every statement of the role shop_app that takes 50 ms or longer, without changing the server-wide 250 ms. Verify it from a shop_app session, then undo it.
In your own session, use auto_explain to log the plan of SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = 42;, and find the plan node in the log.

data.title: Answer
data.text: 1. As postgres: ALTER ROLE shop_app SET log_min_duration_statement = '50ms';. Connect as shop_app and SHOW log_min_duration_statement; returns 50ms. Undo with ALTER ROLE shop_app RESET log_min_duration_statement;. 2. As postgres in database shop: LOAD 'auto_explain'; then SET auto_explain.log_min_duration = 0; and run the query. The log shows an Index Scan using orders_pkey on orders node with Index Cond: (order_id = 42).
Quick reference

data.code:
# Where is the log file of each cluster?
pg_lsclusters

# Follow the log live
sudo tail -f /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log

# Edit logging settings
sudo nano /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf
#   log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d app=%a client=%h '
#   log_min_duration_statement = 250ms
#   log_lock_waits = on
#   log_temp_files = 10MB
#   log_connections = 'authorization,setup_durations'
#   log_disconnections = on

# Apply reloadable settings (no disconnects)
sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main

# Check the values from a new session
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT name, setting, unit FROM pg_settings WHERE name LIKE 'log%' ORDER BY name;"

# Different threshold for one role (and undo)
sudo -u postgres psql -c "ALTER ROLE shop_app SET log_min_duration_statement = '100ms';"
sudo -u postgres psql -c "ALTER ROLE shop_app RESET log_min_duration_statement;"

# Try auto_explain in one session (inside psql as postgres)
#   LOAD 'auto_explain';
#   SET auto_explain.log_min_duration = 0;

# Turn on auto_explain for new sessions
sudo -u postgres nano /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/auto_explain.conf
#   session_preload_libraries = 'auto_explain'
#   auto_explain.log_min_duration = '1s'
#   auto_explain.log_analyze = on
#   auto_explain.log_buffers = on
#   auto_explain.log_timing = off
sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main

# Turn auto_explain off again
sudo rm /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/auto_explain.conf
sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main

# Top 5 slowest logged statements
sudo grep -oE "duration: [0-9.]+ ms  statement: .*" /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log | sort -t' ' -k2 -rn | head -5
data.caption: Every command from this part, in order

data.text: Summary and what's next

items.content: On Ubuntu the server log is /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log (see pg_lsclusters), rotated weekly by logrotate
log_line_prefix with %u, %d, %a and %h makes every line say who, where and from which application
log_min_duration_statement logs slow statements with their text; start around 250 ms to 1 s and set it per role or database when needed
log_lock_waits shows statements that were blocked rather than slow, and log_temp_files shows sorts and hashes that spilled to disk
PostgreSQL 18's log_connections options such as setup_durations show where connection time goes
auto_explain logs the plan of slow statements; load it with session_preload_libraries, keep log_timing off, and test the overhead of log_analyze
Test new library names with LOAD before putting them in a preload setting

data.text: In Part 24 we look at the statistics views every DBA uses: pg_stat_database, pg_stat_user_tables and the pg_statio views.

linkedin.post:
Your app is slow, and PostgreSQL's log shows nothing about it. By default, it isn't recording any of your queries.

Part 23 of my PostgreSQL DBA series is about logging that actually helps. What I set on PostgreSQL 18:

→ log_min_duration_statement = 250ms logs every statement that runs that long, with its full SQL text. Default is -1, off.
→ log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d app=%a client=%h ' so every line says who, which database, which application and from where.
→ log_lock_waits = on. My 3-second single-row UPDATE was not slow, it was blocked. The log named the blocking process.
→ log_temp_files = 10MB shows sorts that spill to disk.
→ auto_explain logs the execution plan of the slow query itself. Load it with session_preload_libraries and keep auto_explain.log_timing off to cut the overhead.

One trap from testing: a typo in session_preload_libraries makes every new connection fail, even postgres. Fix the file and reload from the shell.

What threshold do you use for log_min_duration_statement in production?

Full tutorial with examples: link in the first comment.

points: pg_lsclusters shows the log file per cluster
logging_collector is off, so pg_current_logfile() is NULL

slides.title: Step 2: catch slow statements
slides.body: Statements over the threshold are logged with duration and full SQL text. Lock waits and big temp files tell you why.
slides.code:
log_min_duration_statement = 250ms
log_lock_waits = on
log_temp_files = 10MB

SELECT pg_reload_conf();

slides.title: Step 3: one role, own threshold
points: Applies to new sessions of that role
The app itself cannot switch it off

slides.title: Step 4: plans with auto_explain
points: Test first: LOAD 'auto_explain' in one session
A typo in the name blocks every new login
slides.code:
session_preload_libraries = 'auto_explain'
auto_explain.log_min_duration = '1s'
auto_explain.log_analyze = on
auto_explain.log_timing = off
